name: Carat weight
seoTitle: Carat weight Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Carat weight: work out girdle thickness from the diameter and the width. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Carat weight calculator turns the diameter, the width and more into girdle thickness. It suits whatever you happen to be working on. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Carat weight calculator work?
sections.html:
The Carat weight calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports girdle thickness in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the diamond shape); then you type in the diameter, the width, the depth and the carat weight (Estimated diamond weight).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Carat weight calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Girdle thickness=-1 + (10000 ÷ 61) × carat weight ÷ (depth × (diameter ^ 2))
Weight in other units=carat weight
Girdle thickness=(-depth × length × correction factor × width − depth × length × width + (5000 ÷ 31) × carat weight) ÷ (depth × length × width × (correction factor + 1))
Carat weight=(83 ÷ 10000) × depth × length × width × (girdle thickness × correction factor + girdle thickness + correction factor + 1)
Carat weight=(1 ÷ 125) × depth × length × width × (girdle thickness × correction factor + girdle thickness + correction factor + 1)
Carat weight=weight in other units

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Diamond shape set to Round, Diameter = 30 mm, Depth = 30 mm and Girdle thickness = 0 %. Working through the relationship above gives Weight in other units = 10 g.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Weight in other units = 10 g should be roughly the size you expected from Diamond shape set to Round and Diameter = 30 mm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in millimeters

  • %, opening in percent

  • Mass, opening in carats

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Carat weight calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the diameter, the width and the depth — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Carat weight calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns girdle thickness, derived from the diameter, the width and the depth. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Carat weight calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the diameter, the width, the depth and the carat weight, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter diameter in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Diameter opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Weight in other units = 10 g. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Carat weight calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
